questions.question: Geometrically, the derivative f′(x) at a point is:
options: The area under the curve there
The slope of the tangent line there
The value of the function there
questions.rationale: f′(x) is the limit of secant slopes as the interval shrinks — the tangent line's slope at that exact point.

questions.question: Using the power rule, the derivative of x³ is:
questions.rationale: Bring down the exponent and reduce it by one: d/dx x³ = 3x².

questions.question: If f(x) = 3x⁴ − 2x + 7, then f′(x) =
questions.rationale: Differentiate term by term: 3·4x³ = 12x³, derivative of −2x is −2, constant 7 differentiates to 0.

questions.question: The derivative of a constant (like 7) is:
questions.rationale: Constants never change, so their rate of change is exactly zero.

questions.question: At a point where f′(x) < 0, the function is:
questions.rationale: Negative slope means each small step right drops the output — the function is falling there.

questions.question: A thrown ball has height h(t) = 20t − 5t². When does it reach its peak?
questions.rationale: Peak when h′(t) = 20 − 10t = 0 → t = 2 s; h″ = −10 < 0 confirms a maximum.

questions.question: The peak ball height in the previous problem is:
At a stationary point where f″(x) > 0, the graph has a:
questions.rationale: Zero first derivative marks the flat spot; positive second derivative means the slope is increasing — a valley (minimum).

questions.question: Which function equals its own derivative?
questions.rationale: d/dx eˣ = eˣ — the only elementary function unchanged by differentiation.

questions.question: Why does |x| have no derivative at x = 0?
options: The corner has no single tangent direction
questions.rationale: Left of 0 the slope is −1, right of 0 it is +1; the corner never settles on one tangent, so the limit doesn't exist.
